title: Beliefs
subtitle: adherent, tenet, plausible, take with a pinch of salt
summary: Name the people who hold strong beliefs, describe the principles behind a belief, and judge how believable something is - from credible and plausible to gullible and incredulous.

lesson.heading: People and their beliefs
rows: a person who supports a particular idea or party
someone who has taken on a new set of beliefs
(disapproving) someone with a very strong belief that something is great
someone who believes there should be extreme change, often political
(disapproving) someone opposed to change or new ideas
lesson.note: The noun convert and the verb convert are stressed differently.

lesson.heading: Defining a belief: pacifism
lesson.text: Pacifists **seek to** (want to achieve) **eradicate** violence and conflict - to abolish or get rid of it - and they believe war can never be **justified**. A key **tenet**, a principle on which a belief is based, shared by **proponents** of this way of thinking is that life is precious.

examples.text: Pacifists **seek to eradicate** violence and conflict.
A key **tenet** shared by **proponents** of this way of thinking is that life is precious.
The group felt their protest against the unfair laws was completely **justified**.

lesson.note: A proponent is a person who publicly supports an opinion.

lesson.heading: Where beliefs come from, and how they act
lesson.text: Some pacifists' beliefs **derive from** their religious views - they have their origins in them. Gandhi campaigned for Indian independence through non-violent **civil disobedience**, when a group express disapproval of laws by refusing to obey them. His success inspired others to use peaceful **resistance**, including Martin Luther King Jr.

examples.text: Some pacifists' beliefs **derive from** their religious views.
Gandhi **campaigned** for Indian independence through non-violent **civil disobedience**.
The Government troops offered no **resistance** to the rebel takeover.

lesson.heading: How believable is it?
lesson.text: Something **credible** is believable (opposite **incredible**), and a **plausible** excuse is a convincing one (opposite **implausible**). A **gullible** person is easily tricked into believing things. If you are **incredulous**, you do not want or are not able to believe something.

examples.text: The boy produced a barely **credible** excuse for arriving late.
Can't you find a more **plausible** excuse than that?
He's very **gullible** - he believes anything you tell him.
I was **incredulous** when she told me she was quitting her job to go to New Zealand.

left.label: subjective
left.text: influenced by beliefs or feelings rather than facts
examples: You should try to be less **subjective** about the situation.
The criteria for judging the Poem of the Year competition are, inevitably, to some extent **subjective**.

right.label: objective
right.text: based on facts, not on personal feelings
examples: A judge must try to remain **objective** and not let personal values influence his or her decisions.

lesson.heading: Believing what you are told
lesson.text: To **attribute** something to someone is to consider it to be caused or created by them. To **presume** is to believe something to be true although you are not totally certain. To give someone **the benefit of the doubt** is to accept that they are telling the truth even though it is not certain, and to **take something with a pinch of salt** is not to believe it totally.

examples.text: Many scholars **attribute** this anonymous poem to Dante.
I **presume** that Meena told you what happened.
We should give her the **benefit of the doubt**.
You should take what he says **with a pinch of salt** - he's inclined to exaggerate.

lesson.heading: Your point of view
lesson.text: Your **viewpoint** or **point of view** is your way of thinking about a situation. Do not confuse it with a **tenet**, which is a principle on which a whole belief system rests.

examples.text: Emma's **point of view** is that we should just wait and see what happens next.
Conclude your essay by giving your own **point of view** about what the government should do.

lesson.text: Incredible means unbelievable; incredulous describes the person who cannot believe what they hear.

exercises.prompt: Match each person with the definition of their beliefs.

pairs.right: a person who supports a particular idea or party
someone who has taken on a new set of beliefs
someone with a very strong belief that something is great
someone who believes there should be extreme change
someone opposed to change or new ideas

exercises.prompt: The charity aims to ___ poverty in this region within five years.
exercises.explanation: To eradicate something is to abolish or get rid of it completely.

exercises.prompt: ___ to a religion can often be much more active supporters than people who were born into it.
exercises.explanation: A convert is someone who has taken on a new set of beliefs.

exercises.prompt: The group felt their protest against the unfair laws was completely ___.
exercises.explanation: If an action is justified, there is a good reason for it.

exercises.prompt: Many of the self-professed ___ of this philosophy have never even read its basic texts.
exercises.explanation: An adherent of an idea is a person who supports it.

exercises.prompt: Historians ___ the origins of this philosophy to Ancient Greece.
exercises.explanation: To attribute something to a source is to consider it to be caused or created by that source.

exercises.prompt: The Government troops offered no ___ to the rebel takeover.
exercises.explanation: Resistance is the act of opposing something; peaceful resistance was Gandhi's method.

exercises.prompt: I take anything said by an election candidate with a ___ of salt.
exercises.explanation: To take something with a pinch of salt is not to believe it totally.

exercises.prompt: A gullible person believes everything even if it is ___.
exercises.explanation: Gullible people are easily tricked, so they believe even implausible, unconvincing stories.

exercises.prompt: When marking exams, try to give candidates the ___ of the doubt.
exercises.explanation: To give someone the benefit of the doubt is to accept they are telling the truth even though it is not certain.

exercises.prompt: A judge must try to remain ___ and not let personal values influence his or her decisions.
exercises.explanation: Objective is the opposite of subjective, which means influenced by beliefs or feelings rather than facts.

exercises.statement: The law says that you must be presumed innocent until proven otherwise.
exercises.explanation: Correct - to presume is to believe something to be true although you are not totally certain.

exercises.statement: I don't find his story at all incredulous - it is obviously untrue.
exercises.explanation: I don't find his story at all credible. Incredulous describes a person who cannot believe what they hear.

exercises.prompt: Does each word suggest that something is easy to believe, or hard to believe?

exercises.answer: A tenet is a principle on which a belief is based
exercises.explanation: A key tenet is shared by the proponents of a way of thinking.
